items.content_html:
Beyond the Mirage: a framework for AGI classification and controllable progress

An AI can give an impressive answer about the world without knowing what would happen if it changed that world. It can also act through tools without understanding the consequences of its actions. These are different gaps. Counting parameters does not tell us which one has been crossed.

This framework proposes judging progress towards AGI by verifiable changes in capability: from recognising associations to reasoning about interventions and counterfactuals, and from answering a prompt to pursuing a goal. The Agentic Causal Intelligence framework, or ACI, puts those two dimensions on separate axes. The safety roadmap alongside it asks how our ability to verify and constrain a system can keep pace with what it can do.

The central claim is that we face a Causal Barrier. Robust causal understanding requires more than fluent reproduction of statistical relationships. The gap is a difference in kind, and crossing it calls for a qualitative change in what a system can represent and reason about. Scaling alone is an inadequate account of that change.

Note

This research proposal dates from September 2025; its examples and judgments about models belong to that setting. The strong architectural thesis, ACI classifications and safety roadmap are hypotheses to test; the reported experiments retain the narrower scope stated beside them.

Why bigger isn't necessarily smarter

Large language models learn from enormous bodies of text. They are remarkable navigators of its patterns and correlations. That is mastery of statistical entropy: finding a path through a vast landscape of possible language. But reasoning about the world asks which relationships survive an intervention. A convincing continuation of a sentence and a reliable answer about a changed world are different achievements.1

Two lines of work make parameter count an inadequate answer. The first asks how to spend a training budget. The second asks what a score actually measures.

Chinchilla: size and data must be considered together

DeepMind's 2022 Chinchilla study compared more than 400 training runs. Its compute-optimal analysis found that model size and training tokens should grow in roughly equal proportions. The resulting 70-billion-parameter Chinchilla used 1.4 trillion tokens and the same training compute as the 280-billion-parameter Gopher. It outperformed Gopher on the reported evaluations; its MMLU accuracy was 67.5%, more than seven percentage points higher.2

Parameter count had concealed how the budget was allocated. Training efficiency, data and the cost of using the resulting model belonged in the comparison. The result makes progress an engineering question: what does this allocation of resources actually buy? Its compute-optimal training relation still has to be distinguished from an optimum for a particular inference workload.

That is a useful correction to the spectacle of the ever-larger number. Better engineering can change what the same resources buy. For how that possibility reaches an ordinary business, Evolution of AI, and its future in B2B follows the interface through to the work behind it.

The mirage of emergence

Schaeffer, Miranda and Koyejo's 2023 study offered a measurement explanation for apparently abrupt abilities. A strict all-correct score can stay near zero even while the probability of getting each part right improves. Change the metric, and the same outputs can reveal a smoother progression. They examined arithmetic in the GPT-3/InstructGPT family, metric choices in BIG-Bench, and artificial examples of apparent emergence in vision models.3

Imagine a task with ten independently correct steps, each succeeding with probability pp. Success on the whole task is p10p^{10}. That curve can make a steady improvement in the parts look like a sudden arrival of useful whole-task performance. The example is a calculation under an independence assumption, not a model of every reasoning process.

Before declaring a new kind of intelligence, inspect the metric. The same model outputs can support a story about a sudden leap or a story about steady improvement, depending on how success is counted. That makes measurement part of the explanation, rather than a neutral window onto it.4

Two axes, rather than one ladder of model sizes

The first ACI axis asks what kind of causal question the system can answer. It borrows the distinction between association, intervention and counterfactuals from the causal hierarchy.5

Level 1, association: seeing. What does observing X=xX=x tell us about YY? The expression P(Y∣X=x)P(Y\mid X=x) describes this question. An observation can be informative without being a cause. Seeing an umbrella may predict rain; making someone carry an umbrella does not thereby make it rain.

Level 2, intervention: doing. What happens if XX is deliberately set to xx? Write this as P(Y∣do⁡(X=x))P(Y\mid\operatorname{do}(X=x)). An intervention changes the mechanism determining XX. Recovering its effect needs appropriate causal assumptions or experimental information; an observational distribution alone does not generally determine it.

Level 3, counterfactuals: imagining otherwise. Given what actually happened, what would have happened under a different action? This combines evidence about the actual situation with a model of the alternative. It asks more than an unconditioned prediction about a new intervention.

Those are classes of questions and information. Turning them into an assessment of a deployed AI requires named tasks, assumptions and tests. Producing text containing a causal equation does not establish that the system has solved the corresponding problem.

The second axis asks how the system acts.

Grade A, passive or oracle. A system receives an input and returns an answer. In the proposed classification, a base model used for a single response is the straightforward example. Planning described in an answer is different from authority to execute the plan.

Grade B, reactive or tool-using. The system chooses and uses an external tool within the task. Toolformer is an early research example: it learned when to call APIs, what arguments to supply and how to incorporate the results into subsequent prediction.6 Retrieval and calculators expand what an answer can use. Their availability does not establish causal understanding of the task.

Grade C, proactive or agentic. A system pursues a goal through several steps, maintaining context, planning, inspecting results and revising its approach. AutoGPT-like arrangements illustrate this direction. The unit being classified is the whole arrangement, including memory, tools and permissions, rather than its underlying model in isolation.

The proposed ACI matrix

Cross the axes and the landscape becomes easier to read. A system can move right by gaining tools and autonomy without moving upwards in causal reasoning. The labels below are proposed placements, with the upper cells describing the capabilities we would need to demonstrate.

Causal depth A: passive / oracle B: reactive / tool-using C: proactive / agentic
3: counterfactual Counterfactual oracle Reactive counterfactual agent Proactive counterfactual agent: the proposal's AGI target
2: interventional Interventional oracle; JEPA was suggested as a research direction Reactive interventional agent Proactive interventional agent
1: associative Standard base LLM, illustrated by GPT-3-era use Tool-using LLM, illustrated by Toolformer or RAG Agentic framework, illustrated by AutoGPT-like use

The ACI matrix places these language-model examples on the associative row. Tool use and a planning loop make them more capable agents, but do not by themselves show that their reasoning has crossed into intervention. That upward move is the immediate frontier the framework asks us to confront.

Predictive world models are one promising route. LeCun's JEPA proposal asks how a system could learn representations useful for reasoning and planning.7 It belongs here as a research direction towards an interventional oracle, rather than a certified Level 2 result. A model earns that classification through the questions it can answer.

The notional ACI-3C destination is a proactive agent that can reason counterfactually in pursuit of its objectives. That is the framework's AGI target: autonomy joined to a deeper understanding of what could have happened and what an action would change.

What the causal benchmarks actually test

Fluent models can stumble when a causal question becomes unfamiliar, logically constrained or demanding across several perspectives. These failures motivate the Causal Barrier thesis. We need a scorecard that exposes them, rather than one that lets a persuasive answer stand in for understanding.

Study Evaluated task and population Relevant finding
CausalProbe-2024 Fresh-news causal questions; studied models include LLaMA 2 7B, LLaMA 3 8B, GPT-3.5 Turbo and Claude 3 Opus Performance fell relative to older causal QA benchmarks; the authors also tested a knowledge- and goal-assisted method that improved results.
Corr2Cause More than 200,000 examples generated to test causal inference from correlational statements; seventeen evaluated LLMs The authors report near-random performance and limited out-of-distribution generalisation after fine-tuning.
CausalBench, mathematics GPT-4 Turbo, as named in Table 2 of the paper 88.7% of individual questions correct; 61.4% of scenario groups had all four question types correct.

CausalProbe drew news from the BBC and the Guardian dated 1 January–29 April 2024. Its freshness checks reduce a memorisation concern; they do not make every training exposure independently inspectable. Its “level-1” and “level-2” terminology distinguishes recalled associations from the authors' notion of more genuine reasoning, and must not be substituted automatically for the three Pearl rungs.8

Corr2Cause is a test of reasoning under a constructed set of conditions. Its result does not establish that arbitrary real-world correlations identify a causal relationship. The conditions that make a conclusion follow are part of the problem.9

CausalBench's two percentages use different denominators. The lower score counts success on all four perspectives together: cause to effect, effect to cause, and each with intervention. This is a stricter consistency requirement, not a before-and-after decline on the same measure. The paper separately compares causal scores with a summarisation hallucination leaderboard, including Mistral; that association is not an experiment showing causal skill reduces hallucination.10

These are concrete failures to explain and concrete tests for future systems to improve. The architectural interpretation is that crossing from association to reliable intervention requires a deeper change than another headline model size. The benchmark results locate weaknesses in the tested systems; the architectural interpretation remains the stronger thesis being advanced here.

A roadmap for verification and control

Why make the classification at all? Because an answer, an action and a self-directed sequence of actions create different problems of control. A system that can model consequences more deeply may also find ways around a restriction. The proposal therefore asks that capability and verification develop together.

Yampolskiy's argument about the limits of controlling advanced AI brings the concern into focus: a less capable controller may fail to anticipate or constrain a more capable system.11 We cannot assume that an output filter suitable for an oracle will also control an agent able to plan around it.

The roadmap proposes three layers of work: bounded alignment for associative systems, verifiable process as systems acquire interventional capabilities, and constrained agency for the hypothetical counterfactual agents beyond them. Each layer adds a demand on what we can demonstrate. The roadmap is a research programme, not permission to give a lower-ranked model unchecked tools.12

Bounded alignment

The first layer tries to keep prompts and responses within stated requirements. Constitutional AI's training approach uses principles to guide critique, revision and preference feedback. Llama Guard 3 is a separate example of a model trained to classify input and output content against a safety taxonomy.1314

These techniques can be evaluated against particular unwanted outputs. They do not turn a policy into a guarantee that every output, downstream interpretation or tool action is safe. Their usefulness depends on the requirements, test population and ways they can fail.

The governance side matters too. NIST's AI Risk Management Framework and its July 2024 Generative AI Profile organise risks and responses across a system's lifecycle, including confabulation, harmful bias and information integrity.15 They give an organisation questions to manage and evidence to maintain, rather than certifying a model's ACI level. The EU AI Act is another governance example, with its own risk-based legal categories and duties; those categories are not the ACI matrix.16

Verifiable process

Checking only the final answer is insufficient when the system uses tools or handles protected information. Which program ran? What input did it receive? Which outside action occurred? Was the process altered? Hardware isolation, cryptographic proofs and formal verification can each make a different part of that account inspectable.

Trusted execution environments can isolate a computation from parts of the host under a specified threat model. Intel SGX is one example. Its protections do not cover every side channel, and the application still has to handle vulnerable code, exposed inputs and recovery.17 Protecting a program from alteration is not the same as proving that its decisions are correct.

Zero-knowledge machine learning proposes proofs that a stated computation was carried out without revealing all the underlying private information. A proof of inference can establish execution of the represented model and operation; it does not establish that the model's answer is true or that the chosen objective is acceptable. Proof generation and the faithful representation of the computation introduce costs and assumptions of their own.18

The earlier blockchain essay, A precognition court for AI, explores a related intuition: make relevant operations inspectable and constrain what a system can do through the surrounding arrangement. It is a deliberately abstract argument, not a claim that a ledger solves intelligence or control. The useful question remains what is verified, by whom, and what the verification leaves outside its scope.

Constrained agency

For hypothetical systems with greater autonomy and counterfactual planning, we need to look beyond response filters to constraints on what can be done. Containment, interpretability, corrigibility and limits on resources belong in the research, alongside the physical and computational conditions under which an agent operates. The challenge is to find constraints that remain effective when a system can reason about the constraints themselves.

Energy gives the idea a concrete example. Computation needs infrastructure and power; deployment cannot be detached from those resources. Comparisons with Bitcoin or a country's electricity use make the scale imaginable, but only if the population, period and projected or observed status match. The IEA's April 2025 report estimated 415 TWh for all data centres in 2024 and projected about 945 TWh in its 2030 base case; neither number measures AI alone.19 Energy is a physical constraint any deployed intelligence must face. Turning it into a reliable means of control would require a further argument.

Throughput supplies another analogy. Ethereum has a constrained base layer and a roadmap for scaling through other layers. Its account of danksharding describes a target above 100,000 transactions per second across the scaled system.20 A globally operating intelligence would also need communication, data movement and infrastructure. Those can become bottlenecks even when local computation improves. The Ethereum number is a roadmap target for that network, not a calculated AGI requirement.

What each layer has to establish

Proposed layer Risks motivating the layer Main question Candidate mechanisms and governance work
Bounded alignment, associated with ACI-1 Misinformation, bias, harmful content, confabulation and intellectual-property infringement Do inputs and outputs meet the requirements, and where do they fail? Constitutional training, content classifiers, red teaming, risk assessment and accountable organisational review.
Verifiable process, associated with ACI-2 Unverifiable tool use, process manipulation, data leakage, adversarial attacks and emergent harmful strategies Did the stated computation and permitted actions occur under the declared conditions? Trusted execution, proofs of computation, formal verification, auditable tools, hardware certification and secure APIs.
Constrained agency, associated with ACI-3 Uncontrollability, goal misalignment, instrumental convergence and existential risk What can the system do, resist or circumvent, and which limits remain effective? Containment, interpretability, corrigibility, resource controls, monitoring and research on coordination between institutions.

The policy proposal is to make permission to advance and deploy depend on evidence of appropriate controls. Controls cannot remain something we promise to add after capability. That puts regulatory frameworks, hardware certification and secure APIs alongside possible international arrangements over compute and energy, moratoriums and risk monitoring. These are governance proposals to examine; the benchmark studies do not decide the institutional choices for us.

The transition the framework asks us to measure

AGI dates that leave the definition moving miss this distinction. An increasingly useful tool-using or autonomous assistant may be called AGI while leaving the causal threshold unanswered. Conversely, a narrow system can answer a difficult causal question without having general agency. A date means little until the capability and the test are stated.

The proposed path is a sequence of demanding phase transitions in what can be explained, predicted and done. The phrase expresses a qualitative change in capability; deriving a mathematical phase transition would need a specified model and parameter. The immediate challenge is to master intervention verifiably, alongside the separate growth of autonomy, and to build the corresponding means of control.

The measure of progress should therefore be more than model size or fluent prose. The ambition is robust causal reasoning, demonstrable alignment with the task and control over consequential action. Each needs evidence of its own. A matrix helps only if it makes those demands clearer.

The economic question continues in One Yardstick, One Clock and The Red Pill: even when an agent can do the work, how does the economy adapt, and who can buy what it produces? The mathematical question continues through changing descriptions: which distinctions must a model retain to answer the next question? The ineffable geometry and Entropy and a learning mind approach that question from the earlier geometric and learning intuitions.

Yay, you made it to the end. Congratulations.

  1. “Statistical entropy” expresses the opening intuition. This argument does not define an entropy measure that ranks causal understanding against language modelling. ↩

  2. Hoffmann et al., Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models, 2022, and DeepMind's account of the experiment. ↩

  3. Schaeffer, Miranda and Koyejo, Are Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models a Mirage?, NeurIPS 2023. ↩

  4. The metric result concerns the studied tasks and model families. It does not prove that every future capability is predictable. A smoothly crossed threshold can still change which complete tasks a system can perform. ↩

  5. Shpitser and Pearl, Complete Identification Methods for the Causal Hierarchy, JMLR 9, 2008. ↩

  6. Schick et al., Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools, 2023. ↩

  7. LeCun, A Path Towards Autonomous Machine Intelligence, position paper, 27 June 2022. ↩

  8. Chi et al., Unveiling Causal Reasoning in Large Language Models: Reality or Mirage?, preprint v1, 26 June 2025, especially sections 6.1–6.3 and the limitations. ↩

  9. Jin et al., Can Large Language Models Infer Causation from Correlation?, ICLR 2024. ↩

  10. Wang, CausalBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Evaluating Causal Reasoning Capabilities of Large Language Models, SIGHAN-10, 16 August 2024; mathematics Table 2 and the separate hallucination comparison in section 4. ↩

  11. Yampolskiy, On Controllability of AI, 2020. ↩

  12. Causal depth and access to act are separate in the matrix. A tool-using ACI-1B or proactive ACI-1C arrangement can already have consequential effects. The three research layers therefore do not supply a sufficient control policy for each deployment merely from its causal row. ↩

  13. Bai et al., Constitutional AI: Harmlessness from AI Feedback, 2022. ↩

  14. Meta, Llama Guard 3 8B model card, describing the 2024 model. ↩

  15. NIST, Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile, July 2024. ↩

  16. European Commission, AI Act. The law supplies its own classification and application timetable; this proposal does not infer a legal category from an ACI cell. ↩

  17. Intel, Intel SGX SDK for Linux overview, including its stated side-channel limitation; consulted 16 November 2026. ↩

  18. A Survey of Zero-Knowledge Proof Based Verifiable Machine Learning, 2025, reviewing work through December 2024. ↩

  19. IEA, Energy and AI: executive summary, April 2025. The population is all data centres; the 2030 value is a projection. ↩

  20. Ethereum, Danksharding, consulted 16 November 2026; the quoted capacity is a roadmap goal. ↩

Energy is a physical constraint any deployed intelligence must face. Turning it into a reliable means of control would require a further argument.
Throughput supplies another analogy. Ethereum has a constrained base layer and a roadmap for scaling through other layers. Its account of danksharding describes a target above 100,000 transactions per second across the scaled system. A globally operating intelligence would also need communication, data movement and infrastructure. Those can become bottlenecks even when local computation improves. The Ethereum number is a roadmap target for that network, not a calculated AGI requirement.
What each layer has to establish
Proposed layer	Risks motivating the layer	Main question	Candidate mechanisms and governance work	
Bounded alignment, associated with ACI-1	Misinformation, bias, harmful content, confabulation and intellectual-property infringement	Do inputs and outputs meet the requirements, and where do they fail?	Constitutional training, content classifiers, red teaming, risk assessment and accountable organisational review.	
Verifiable process, associated with ACI-2	Unverifiable tool use, process manipulation, data leakage, adversarial attacks and emergent harmful strategies	Did the stated computation and permitted actions occur under the declared conditions?	Trusted execution, proofs of computation, formal verification, auditable tools, hardware certification and secure APIs.	
Constrained agency, associated with ACI-3	Uncontrollability, goal misalignment, instrumental convergence and existential risk	What can the system do, resist or circumvent, and which limits remain effective?	Containment, interpretability, corrigibility, resource controls, monitoring and research on coordination between institutions.	
The policy proposal is to make permission to advance and deploy depend on evidence of appropriate controls. Controls cannot remain something we promise to add after capability. That puts regulatory frameworks, hardware certification and secure APIs alongside possible international arrangements over compute and energy, moratoriums and risk monitoring. These are governance proposals to examine; the benchmark studies do not decide the institutional choices for us.
The transition the framework asks us to measure
AGI dates that leave the definition moving miss this distinction. An increasingly useful tool-using or autonomous assistant may be called AGI while leaving the causal threshold unanswered. Conversely, a narrow system can answer a difficult causal question without having general agency. A date means little until the capability and the test are stated.
The proposed path is a sequence of demanding phase transitions in what can be explained, predicted and done. The phrase expresses a qualitative change in capability; deriving a mathematical phase transition would need a specified model and parameter. The immediate challenge is to master intervention verifiably, alongside the separate growth of autonomy, and to build the corresponding means of control.
The measure of progress should therefore be more than model size or fluent prose. The ambition is robust causal reasoning, demonstrable alignment with the task and control over consequential action. Each needs evidence of its own. A matrix helps only if it makes those demands clearer.
The economic question continues in One Yardstick, One Clock and The Red Pill: even when an agent can do the work, how does the economy adapt, and who can buy what it produces? The mathematical question continues through changing descriptions: which distinctions must a model retain to answer the next question? The ineffable geometry and Entropy and a learning mind approach that question from the earlier geometric and learning intuitions.
Yay, you made it to the end. Congratulations.
“Statistical entropy” expresses the opening intuition. This argument does not define an entropy measure that ranks causal understanding against language modelling.
Hoffmann et al., Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models, 2022, and DeepMind's account of the experiment.
Schaeffer, Miranda and Koyejo, Are Emergent Abilities of Large Language Models a Mirage?, NeurIPS 2023.
The metric result concerns the studied tasks and model families. It does not prove that every future capability is predictable. A smoothly crossed threshold can still change which complete tasks a system can perform.
Shpitser and Pearl, Complete Identification Methods for the Causal Hierarchy, JMLR 9, 2008.
Schick et al., Toolformer: Language Models Can Teach Themselves to Use Tools, 2023.
LeCun, A Path Towards Autonomous Machine Intelligence, position paper, 27 June 2022.
Chi et al., Unveiling Causal Reasoning in Large Language Models: Reality or Mirage?, preprint v1, 26 June 2025, especially sections 6.1–6.3 and the limitations.
Jin et al., Can Large Language Models Infer Causation from Correlation?, ICLR 2024.
Wang, CausalBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Evaluating Causal Reasoning Capabilities of Large Language Models, SIGHAN-10, 16 August 2024; mathematics Table 2 and the separate hallucination comparison in section 4.
Yampolskiy, On Controllability of AI, 2020.
Causal depth and access to act are separate in the matrix. A tool-using ACI-1B or proactive ACI-1C arrangement can already have consequential effects. The three research layers therefore do not supply a sufficient control policy for each deployment merely from its causal row.
Bai et al., Constitutional AI: Harmlessness from AI Feedback, 2022.
Meta, Llama Guard 3 8B model card, describing the 2024 model.
NIST, Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile, July 2024.
European Commission, AI Act. The law supplies its own classification and application timetable; this proposal does not infer a legal category from an ACI cell.
Intel, Intel SGX SDK for Linux overview, including its stated side-channel limitation; consulted 16 November 2026.
A Survey of Zero-Knowledge Proof Based Verifiable Machine Learning, 2025, reviewing work through December 2024.
IEA, Energy and AI: executive summary, April 2025. The population is all data centres; the 2030 value is a projection.
Ethereum, Danksharding, consulted 16 November 2026; the quoted capacity is a roadmap goal.

items.title: Entropy and a learning mind
items.content_html:
Entropy and a learning mind

A coffee mug can shatter into pieces. We do not expect the pieces to jump back together and become a mug. You do not need to be a physics or mathematics nerd to carry that expectation. Nerds have tools and labels for describing what you already find intuitive.

That familiar asymmetry led to a question I wrote about in January 2024. Could a neural network begin with a useful intuition about the problem it faces, rather than having to discover every regularity from scratch? And if it kept learning from a stream of feedback, what would happen to the special arrangement that carried the intuition?

The question connects an image from thermodynamics with learning. It is an analogy to investigate, not a thermodynamic law for neural-network weights.

What the mug helps us see

One way into entropy is to count the microscopic arrangements consistent with a macroscopic description. In the equal-probability setting, Boltzmann's expression is S=kBlog⁡ΩS=k_B\log\Omega, where Ω\Omega is that count. Many microscopic arrangements can fit what we describe as the shattered mug; the familiar intact arrangement is more constrained. The count depends on the state and description being considered, so “disorder” is an intuition rather than a definition sufficient for every use of entropy.1

Think of a low-entropy arrangement as a special state, then ask why a system tends to leave it. The picture needs a system boundary and assumptions about its dynamics. The second law concerns total entropy for an isolated system; local order can increase while energy and entropy are exchanged with an environment. A refrigerator and a living organism do not contradict it merely by maintaining an organised part.

Still, the mug makes the temporal intuition vivid. We expect some changes in one direction and regard their reversal as extraordinarily unlikely under ordinary conditions. That expectation informs how we read a cause and its aftermath. It does not, on its own, supply a complete theory of causation.

Begin with an intuition, then keep learning

Imagine a large model whose initial weights or architecture carry a useful regularity about the task. Perhaps it begins with a bias that helps it recognise the relevant structure, instead of treating every possible pattern alike. The training then continues, in real time, as the system receives new observations and feedback.

The weights are an arrangement that makes some responses possible and others unlikely. Will continued adaptation preserve the useful intuition, refine it or wash it out?

An aligned prior could make learning more efficient. A mistaken prior could send the model towards a poor solution or make new evidence harder to absorb. Neither consequence follows just from giving the system more information. The initial arrangement, the task and the update rule interact.

Continued learning could spread those weights into a less special state, perhaps making the model more general. That is a hypothesis about learning dynamics, not something the second law establishes. A weight distribution needs a defined measure before we can speak precisely about its entropy; performance and that measure need not move together. Training also supplies an objective and repeated interventions, rather than leaving an isolated physical system to evolve freely.

Losing a bias and losing a capability are different changes

Suppose the initial intuition is helpful for yesterday's task and wrong for today's. Relaxing it might be learning. Suppose it is still needed, but the latest feedback overwrites it. Then the same movement away from the initial state might be forgetting.

This makes the question more interesting than whether the weights changed. What did the change let the model do, and what could it no longer do? Can it retain a useful old response while adapting to a new one? Does the cost of preserving the old capability prevent the new learning?

Continual-learning research already studies this problem through catastrophic forgetting and the balance between stability and adaptation. One example, elastic weight consolidation, slows changes to weights estimated to matter for earlier tasks.2 It gives a concrete mechanism to compare with the early intuition; it does not establish that all useful knowledge occupies a neatly extractable part of a model.

Then there is irreversibility. Once training leaves a useful arrangement, will the process naturally return to it? A saved checkpoint can restore parameters, but that is an external recovery procedure, not the learning dynamics reversing themselves. Reaching the same performance later is another claim again: a different internal arrangement might solve the same test.

A continuously adapting system needs a continuing comparison

Complexity adds to the difficulty. A change in one part of a network can affect several tasks, and a stream of new feedback can change which skills matter. The model may improve on its immediate objective while losing a property that was important to the larger system. Continuous adaptation is both the attraction and the problem.

That makes monitoring more than watching a training loss fall. The comparison needs the useful behaviour we wanted to retain, the new behaviour we wanted to acquire, the resources spent on each and the conditions under which either stops working. Otherwise “more general” becomes a description we apply after the change without a test that distinguishes improvement from drift.

MUON's account of experience separates a changed immediate state, a retained record and learning across episodes. Reckon's local laboratory supplies a narrower experiment: compare memory rules or budgets on a stated task and inspect what was kept and what happened. They give connected questions forms in which a result can be inspected.

The earlier geometry thought experiment asked whether a better language could make causal relationships intelligible. Beyond the Mirage later asks what evidence would distinguish causal understanding from successful association. This essay sits between them with a simpler question: can we build a system around useful intuitions without losing what made them useful as the system changes?

A mug's fate seems obvious. A learning system is less obliging. We have to define the special state, observe the change and test the capability. That is where the analogy becomes an experiment worth doing.

The autocorrect paradox approaches the problem through a decade of building AI products: why does a model keep getting almost good enough, and what work remains before it fits the task?

  1. David Tong, Statistical Physics, lecture notes on statistical mechanics and thermodynamics. The counting expression requires its stated statistical setting; the learning analogy supplies no independent entropy law. ↩

  2. Kirkpatrick et al., Overcoming catastrophic forgetting in neural networks, 2016 preprint, published in PNAS in 2017. The work tests a particular retention method, not universal recovery of earlier knowledge. ↩

items.title: The future can constrain a model without sending a message back
items.content_text:
The future can constrain a model without sending a message back
A destination changes how we plan a journey. A terminal condition can also change a mathematical path everywhere along its course. Both invite a question: what happens when we describe a stretch of history together with the futures it admits, rather than describing only an isolated present state?
The answer depends on what the future contributes to the construction. Planning uses predictions to choose an action now. A boundary-value problem specifies conditions at more than one point and asks for a whole path consistent with them. An advanced equation explicitly contains the state at a later time. These give three different ways to formulate a temporal question. They require different data and support different conclusions.
An endpoint is a constraint, not an observation from tomorrow
Consider continuously differentiable paths x on [0,1] with x(0)=0 and x(1)=1. Minimise E[x]=\int_0^1(x'(t))^2\,dt. Write x(t)=t+u(t) with u(0)=u(1)=0. Then

E[x]=\int_0^1(1+u')^2\,dt
=1+2\bigl(u(1)-u(0)\bigr)+\int_0^1(u')^2\,dt
=1+\int_0^1(u')^2\,dt.

The remaining integral is non-negative. Equality requires u'=0 throughout; the endpoints then force u=0. Thus x(t)=t is the unique minimiser in this class. The proof identifies both the solution and why no bent path can tie it.
The straight path minimises energy among three curves that share the same two endpoints.
The plotted family is x(t)=t+a\sin(\pi t), with a=0,0.2,-0.2. Every path satisfies the same endpoint data, while E=1+a^2\pi^2/2. The bent paths remain admissible; the energy criterion selects the straight one.
The terminal condition affects the solution everywhere. We supplied both endpoints as part of the problem, rather than obtaining tomorrow's measured endpoint today. Different endpoint data define a different problem. What is solved together is the path: each local value belongs to a trajectory satisfying the given conditions and minimising the stated energy.
That makes the elementary example useful beyond its simplicity. It shows how a whole-path question can constrain local behaviour through consistency, without a mechanism that sends information backwards. The future enters as a condition on the admissible solution, and its role is explicit enough to examine.
Predicting is another construction
A planner can simulate candidate actions, score their predicted consequences and choose one. Its predictions may be mistaken because the action at the present time depends on an available model of the future, not an observation of the actual future. The prediction and objective are the information available for that choice. Comparing the actions they select and the outcomes that follow tests their usefulness; the actual future remains something the planner will encounter, including the consequences its model missed.
An equation containing x(t+\tau) makes a different commitment. One must specify a domain, admissible solution class and boundary data, and establish whether a solution exists or is unique. Inconsistency or non-uniqueness is a possible mathematical outcome. Physical realisation would be a further question about that particular model.
The boundary changes the representation of a local state
A linear example exposes where the supplied information sits. For y'(t)=-\lambda y(t)+f(t) with \lambda>0 and initial data at t_0, the solution is

y(t)=e^{-\lambda(t-t_0)}y(t_0)+\int_{t_0}^t e^{-\lambda(t-s)}f(s)\,ds.

The current value is written in terms of an initial state and a weighted history of forcing. Specify the terminal value at T instead, and the same equation can be written

y(t)=e^{\lambda(T-t)}y(T)-\int_t^T e^{\lambda(s-t)}f(s)\,ds.

This second representation uses future forcing and a terminal condition because those are the data we supplied. It has not made them available to a real-time observer. The growing coefficient also exposes the instability of reconstructing an earlier state through a noisy record: a small terminal error is magnified as the reconstructed interval lengthens. A formula for a path and a procedure that can reliably obtain it from available observations are different achievements.
Eliminating an unobserved linear component from a larger model can leave a history integral or a future-conditioned integral in the remaining variables, depending on how that component was anchored. That is a mathematical route to temporal nonlocality in a reduced description. It still requires the larger equations and their data. Conversely, an equation that mixes delayed and advanced states cannot be justified by the existence of either representation above: its well-posedness is its own question, and resonant or inconsistent boundary data can prevent a solution in the declared class.
A description along a path
The wider ambition is to understand how the path taken changes what a description needs to preserve. Two states may answer the same questions now and give different answers after an allowed continuation. A terminal condition may rule out a path that otherwise looks locally admissible. A model adequate for one predicted future may fail when another becomes relevant. These are connected intuitions, but they are not the same mathematical relation.
MONAD investigates descriptions, probes and the continuations a description permits; its temporal branch asks how planning, whole-trajectory constraints and literal advanced states fit into that inquiry. How the three connect remains research work. The endpoint calculation supplies one exact construction, not a theory of every temporal dependence or a physical demonstration of retrocausation.
What makes the question promising is the possibility of following a local description through a larger stretch of permitted change. Instead of giving the future a mysterious influence, we can ask which paths remain possible, which information their selection requires, and where a present description ceases to be enough.

items.title: The ineffable geometry
items.content_html:
The ineffable geometry

Okay, let's run a hypothetical thought experiment. You are participating in a tribe's discussion. There's a catch: you don't understand their vocabulary, and they don't understand yours. Where do you begin?

That is the difficulty of finding a mathematical language for causality: a relationship can seem within reach before there is a way to state it. It stops making sense pretty fast.

Mathematics and our understanding of the physical world have developed together. Calculus gives us a language for motion and change. Vector calculus helps describe fields. Tensor methods let us express geometry without tying everything to a particular coordinate system. The interesting part is not a tidy history in which each tool appeared for one purpose. It is that a better language can make a previously awkward question possible to ask precisely.

Could a richer geometric language help articulate causality, especially where quantum theory, complex systems and AI make ordinary intuition unreliable? What would that language let us see?

From knowing a number to realising what it means

Take another thought experiment. Suppose I tell you that a thousand children die each day for want of clean water. This is a stipulated number for the image, not a mortality estimate. You hear it and say: that's a lot.

Now imagine those thousand bodies lined up along your way home from work. Imagine that happening for ten years: 10×365×100010\times365\times1000 bodies, in this simplified count. Now imagine, God forbid, that one is someone you love.

The number has not changed. Your relationship to it has. Knowing, understanding and realising are doing different work here. The distance between a quantity and a lived consequence has become difficult to ignore.

The words murti and darshan suggest another way to approach that distance. In this image, the seeker comes to a form through a realisation, not merely through a label. “Idol” does not carry that distinction. This interpretation does not settle the words’ different religious meanings.

Geometry offered a mathematical counterpart to that wish: a way to see a relationship rather than only manipulate its symbols. A derivative becomes a slope; an integral becomes an accumulated area. The picture does not replace the definition or proof. It can help us realise what the definition is saying.

What would a geometry of causality let us do?

The ambition is a calculus whose geometry makes causal relationships more directly intelligible. Determinism is the holy grail here: an account precise enough to explain a mechanism rather than leave every question at a correlation. That aspiration does not establish that nature must be deterministic, or that probability and statistics have become unnecessary.

Indirect evidence seemed a useful starting point. We infer an unseen object from what it changes around it; the bending of light can reveal something about the mass between us and its source. Could a similar discipline help locate a causal relationship that cannot be inspected directly? Statistical causal inference already develops ways of asking such questions. The wider inquiry was whether insights from physics, mathematics, philosophy, computation and cognition could supply other useful descriptions.

Time symmetry was one possible direction. A law can admit a reversed description while the observations and boundary conditions available to us privilege one direction. Another was to make temporal relationships less dependent on the picture of an isolated present moving along a line. A third was simulation: specify a proposed rule, examine what follows, and find where the construction fails. A simulated effect would establish something about the rule supplied, not demonstrate that the physical world follows it.

Could a local mathematical account of intelligence let us isolate and transfer useful pieces of it? The idea of “micro-calculus” is to look closely enough at a system's changes to make a capability transferable in parts. The name supplies no method yet. Defining the unit, the preserved capability and the transformation would be part of the research.

That possibility matters beyond a clever model. If a system's reasoning and changes became more intelligible, it could help with reliability, engineering, public policy and decisions about AI. The chain from a new description to those applications remains work to establish.

More than a line

Two days later, on 24 December 2023, I took the hunch into another thought experiment. This is my favourite kind: bring a few tangents together and see what breaks. Ready?

Is the sum of a triangle's interior angles always 180 degrees?

For an ordinary triangle in Euclidean plane geometry, yes. On a curved surface, the corresponding rule can differ. A triangle on a sphere, following great-circle arcs from the North Pole to two points on the equator ninety degrees apart, has three right angles. Its sum is 270 degrees. The surface and the meaning of its straightest paths are part of the question.

The comparison has a third case: on a hyperbolic plane, a geodesic triangle's angles add to less than 180 degrees. Positive, zero and negative curvature give different answers to the apparently familiar question. The NASA comparison of a sphere, a flat plane and a saddle is a way into that distinction; specifying the geometry is what makes the answer precise.

Now ask: what is the dimension of time?

We know how to measure the dimensions of a phone or a room. Seconds, minutes and hours measure duration. But a unit of duration does not by itself tell us what kind of mathematical object time should be in a particular theory. Nor does uncertainty about that question mean that physics knows nothing about time.

For the sake of the obnoxious experiment, suppose time could be described using a fractional dimension and a non-Euclidean geometry. What would a line through that space look like?

In this image, it bends, loops, disappears and appears before it begins. Could understanding such a line tell us something about the flow of time, and could a framework make sense of an effect preceding its cause? Retrocausality was the question, not an established consequence of the picture.

Fractional dimension, curvature and causal order are different mathematical properties. Choosing the first two does not derive the third. To turn this image into a model, we would have to say what the space is, what counts as a path, how events are ordered, what observations are available and which equations relate them. Only then could we test consistency or ask what the construction predicts.

It is a challenging picture to wrap your head around. I don't blame you if it doesn't make sense. Hence the name ineffable geometry: the intuition comes before an adequate language for it.

A hunch with work in front of it

As much as I hate to admit it, this is, at best, a hunch: the geometry of time might connect chaos, entropy, causality and consciousness. It needs mathematical rigour, beginning with a search for inconsistencies in its own assumptions.

The next exploration, Entropy and a learning mind, asks what happens when a trained system's useful initial arrangement keeps changing. A later, narrower calculation, The future can constrain a model without sending a message back, shows exactly how supplied endpoint data can constrain a whole path. There, the future enters through the data supplied to the problem. The larger question is how to describe time and causal order themselves.

MONAD is where that idea of micro-calculus now lives, under the name it grew into: which answers a description preserves, and when the objects or rules of that description need to change. The geometric ambition is larger than any one existing example. Its value will depend on what it eventually lets us state, derive and test.

I am brewing the idea. The invitation is to explore it seriously enough to discover both what is promising and what does not survive the mathematics. The object of the thought experiment is more than a line. The line is where the work starts.

The ineffable geometry
Okay, let's run a hypothetical thought experiment. You are participating in a tribe's discussion. There's a catch: you don't understand their vocabulary, and they don't understand yours. Where do you begin?
That is the difficulty of finding a mathematical language for causality: a relationship can seem within reach before there is a way to state it. It stops making sense pretty fast.
Mathematics and our understanding of the physical world have developed together. Calculus gives us a language for motion and change. Vector calculus helps describe fields. Tensor methods let us express geometry without tying everything to a particular coordinate system. The interesting part is not a tidy history in which each tool appeared for one purpose. It is that a better language can make a previously awkward question possible to ask precisely.
Could a richer geometric language help articulate causality, especially where quantum theory, complex systems and AI make ordinary intuition unreliable? What would that language let us see?
From knowing a number to realising what it means
Take another thought experiment. Suppose I tell you that a thousand children die each day for want of clean water. This is a stipulated number for the image, not a mortality estimate. You hear it and say: that's a lot.
Now imagine those thousand bodies lined up along your way home from work. Imagine that happening for ten years: 10\times365\times1000 bodies, in this simplified count. Now imagine, God forbid, that one is someone you love.
The number has not changed. Your relationship to it has. Knowing, understanding and realising are doing different work here. The distance between a quantity and a lived consequence has become difficult to ignore.
The words murti and darshan suggest another way to approach that distance. In this image, the seeker comes to a form through a realisation, not merely through a label. “Idol” does not carry that distinction. This interpretation does not settle the words’ different religious meanings.
Geometry offered a mathematical counterpart to that wish: a way to see a relationship rather than only manipulate its symbols. A derivative becomes a slope; an integral becomes an accumulated area. The picture does not replace the definition or proof. It can help us realise what the definition is saying.

items.title: The record and the arrow
items.content_html:
The record and the arrow

The trace is still there: a sensor value, an image, a stored summary. Following it backwards seems like a matter of undoing what happened. Yet a perfectly reversible motion can leave a record compatible with several different beginnings. Where did the ambiguity enter if the motion itself lost nothing? The answer lies in the whole route from the state to the record, including what the observer could see and keep.

This is one reason the observer belongs inside a description of the problem. Not because attention changes physical law, but because resolution, noise, preparation and permitted operations change which questions a record can answer. A finite budget can make a distinction unreachable even when it still exists in the underlying system.

The record-and-observer account began in Reckon's February 2026 framework. Its retrodiction chapter separates identifiability, inverse sensitivity and noise before deriving the logarithmic horizon. The calculation here develops that distinction for a reader who need not run the laboratory.

Reversing the dynamics does not reverse the channel

Write an effective observation as

Oτ,R,s=CR∘Πs∘Φτ∘U. O_{\tau,R,s}=C_R\circ\Pi_s\circ\Phi_\tau\circ U.

Here UU is an allowed preparation, Φτ\Phi_\tau the evolution over time τ\tau, Πs\Pi_s the observation scale and CRC_R the record channel available under resources RR. Reconstructing an earlier state requires the relevant information to survive the whole composition. Inverting Φτ\Phi_\tau alone cannot undo distinctions that Πs\Pi_s erased.

A finite example makes this exact. Rotate a three-bit state so that (a,b,c) becomes (b,c,a), then record only its first bit. The rotation is reversible, but the record 0 has four possible earlier states because it tells us only that b=0. With all three output bits, the past is uniquely recoverable. With one bit, it is not. Extra precision in that one bit cannot recover a or c; another observation is needed. Non-identifiability is not merely a difficult numerical inversion.

A unique inverse can still amplify error

Now consider yτ=e−λτx0y_\tau=e^{-\lambda\tau}x_0, with λ>0\lambda>0 and bounded observation error ∣ξ∣≤σ|\xi|\leq\sigma. The map is injective at every finite τ\tau, but its inverse amplifies error:

x^0=eλτ(yτ+ξ),∣x^0−x0∣≤eλτσ. \hat x_0=e^{\lambda\tau}(y_\tau+\xi), \qquad |\hat x_0-x_0|\leq e^{\lambda\tau}\sigma.

For a fixed noise bound and required error ε≥σ\varepsilon\geq\sigma, the worst-case guarantee holds only while

τ≤log⁡(ε/σ)λ. \tau\leq\frac{\log(\varepsilon/\sigma)}{\lambda}.

This horizon comes from conditioning of the inverse, not from a many-to-one evolution.

Take λ=1 per unit of time, σ=0.001 and an allowed reconstruction error of 0.1. The worst-case guarantee reaches about 4.605 time units. Reducing the noise bound tenfold adds about 2.303 units; it does not multiply the horizon tenfold. A noiseless channel, a differently conditioned map or a different observable changes the result. The useful distinction is between information that never survived the record and information that survived but becomes increasingly expensive to recover accurately.

That makes a record design a question about future use. More stored detail is valuable when it preserves a distinction the later reconstruction needs. Repeated measurements can help only under an appropriate noise model; correlated errors need not average away. A log with perfect byte retention can still omit the preparation, the observation scale or the event needed to interpret its values.

Entropy depends on the description being counted

For a closed system evolving by a measure-preserving reversible map, the fine-grained entropy of the transported distribution is unchanged, when that entropy is well defined. A macrostate instead groups many microstates. Its Boltzmann entropy is

SB(m)=kBlog⁡μ(Γm), S_B(m)=k_B\log\mu(\Gamma_m),

where Γm\Gamma_m is the set of microstates in macrostate mm, μ\mu is the measure the map preserves and kBk_B is Boltzmann's constant. These are different objects. A macrostate can become more typical without the fine-grained distribution acquiring or destroying information in the same sense.

Lebowitz's account of Boltzmann's entropy and time's arrow explains how macroscopic irreversibility can coexist with reversible microscopic dynamics. Coarse and fine descriptions, a low-entropy past and typicality matter to that explanation. Reversibility by itself does not supply a theorem that every observation has an arrow, nor does naming a learning loss “entropy” make it a thermodynamic quantity.

The observer-relative question is consequently more precise than “is the past lost?” Which distinction was recorded, through which channel, at what scale, and which inverse problem is being attempted? Given endpoint data can constrain a path because the information is part of the problem. A trace has to preserve the information from which the path might be recovered. The past can remain unique in the dynamics while several pasts remain compatible with the record.

items.title: When effects cancel along a path
items.content_html:
When effects cancel along a path

An intervention on A changes B. An intervention on B changes C. It is tempting to conclude that intervening on A changes C. That conclusion need not hold. A path records relationships under particular interventions; it does not ensure that their effects compose without cancellation.

Take the binary structural model

A∼Bernoulli⁡(1/4),B=A,C=A⊕B. A\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/4),\qquad B=A,\qquad C=A\oplus B.

The symbol ⊕\oplus denotes xor. In the unmodified system CC is always zero.

Set A to zero or one by intervention and leave the other equations intact. B changes from zero to one. C remains zero, because its two inputs change together and cancel under xor. A therefore has a detectable effect on B but no distributional effect on C in this comparison.

Now intervene on B, replacing its equation while leaving A’s distribution unchanged. Setting B to zero makes C equal A, so C is one with probability one quarter. Setting B to one makes C the complement of A, so C is one with probability three quarters. B has a detectable effect on C, yet the earlier A-to-C conclusion still fails. The intervention on B breaks a dependency that the intervention on A preserved. That difference is enough to produce the failure in this constructed model.

What each intervention does to C

Intervention Assignments A ⊕ B = C, with probability Probability C = 1
Set A = 0 0 ⊕ 0 = 0 (100%) 0%
Set A = 1 1 ⊕ 1 = 0 (100%) 0%
Set B = 0 0 ⊕ 0 = 0 (75%); 1 ⊕ 0 = 1 (25%) 25%
Set B = 1 0 ⊕ 1 = 1 (75%); 1 ⊕ 1 = 0 (25%) 75%

Reachability and direct evidence are different relations

A graph algorithm can compute transitive reachability. That is a valid operation on graph structure. Reinterpreting every reachable pair as a directly detectable intervention effect is a separate operation requiring assumptions the graph alone does not contain.

A debugger can use inferred paths to choose which relationships to examine next, while retaining measured edges as a separate relation. Testing an implied edge costs trials and supplies its own comparison. The graph becomes an instrument for investigation when reachability directs attention without replacing the evidence that an intervention needs.

Reliable does not mean detectable at every threshold

Suppose a binary channel records a balanced input correctly with probability 0.8. Under input zero it records one with probability 0.2; under input one that probability is 0.8. The total-variation distance between these two output laws is 0.6.

A stipulated detection threshold of 0.9 is not met even though prediction through the channel succeeds eighty percent of the time. Reliability and detection refer to different criteria. Improving a record does not license every threshold or erase the conditions under which it was observed.

Joseph Halpern gives a finite counterexample to the transitivity of causation, alongside conditions that can restore it.1 His counterexample prompted a separate check in MONAD’s own finite observer model.

The MONAD programme includes a machine-checked failure of transitivity in its finite observer setting. Detectable influence in that setting cannot simply be treated as an order. Taking its transitive closure would add relationships whose intervention effects need to be examined separately.

The xor example shows what such a check can reveal. One intervention breaks a dependency that another preserves, so the two paths carry different evidence. An account of those intervention-specific relationships is more informative than a larger graph whose edges have silently changed meaning.

  1. Joseph Y. Halpern, Sufficient Conditions for Causality to Be Transitive, 2016. The check uses his displayed three-variable equations under hard interventions; it does not identify his definition of actual causation with MONAD’s detectable influence. The checked MONAD example fixes the starting state at (0,0,0) and allows only the identity operation and four specified maps that set A or B, with noiseless records. This article instead uses Bernoulli-distributed A and interventions that replace a structural equation to illustrate the same cancellation. ↩

items.content_html:
When the support moves

“With more samples, we can detect smaller changes.” But how much smaller? Suppose an instrument produces independent measurements uniformly between zero and an endpoint θ. Another setting moves that endpoint slightly. Most readings could have come from either setting; one reading beyond the old endpoint could not. That sharp edge gives another sample an opportunity unlike the one it has in a smooth shift of an average.

We can calculate what the opportunity is worth. Let the original law be uniform on [0, θ], with θ positive, and compare it with a uniform law on a slightly longer interval. The endpoint changes which observations are possible. Following that change through a two-hypothesis test gives a detection scale that sample count alone would not tell us.

A single observation can rule out one hypothesis

Call the original endpoint θ\theta and the alternative endpoint θ+δ\theta+\delta, with δ>0\delta>0. If any observation exceeds θ\theta, it is impossible under the original law. If every observation lies below θ\theta, both laws remain possible.

Under the alternative, one observation lies below θ\theta with probability θ/(θ+δ)\theta/(\theta+\delta). For nn independent observations, the probability that all remain below it is

qn=(θθ+δ)n. q_n=\left(\frac{\theta}{\theta+\delta}\right)^n.

The support boundary is doing the work. Yibi Huang's parameter-estimation lecture uses the uniform-endpoint family to show why a sample maximum constrains which endpoints have nonzero likelihood. Here we use that same boundary for a two-hypothesis test rather than estimate an unrestricted endpoint.

The optimal balanced test has an exact error

Give the two hypotheses equal prior probability and charge the same loss for either wrong answer. On the common region, the original law has the greater joint density: θ−n\theta^{-n} rather than (θ+δ)−n(\theta+\delta)^{-n}. Outside it, only the alternative can occur.

The optimal decision is therefore original when all observations are at most θ\theta, alternative otherwise. It never mistakes the original law for the alternative. Under the alternative, it is wrong with probability qnq_n. Averaging over the equal priors gives total error qn/2q_n/2.

This is a complete calculation for the declared test. It is not an empirical error estimate or a guarantee for an unknown population. Different priors or unequal losses would change the decision threshold.

An inverse-sample change remains detectable

Now let the alternative depend on sample count: set δ=h/n\delta=h/n, for fixed h>0h>0. Then

qn=(1+hnθ)−n⟶e−h/θ,balanced error⟶12e−h/θ. q_n=\left(1+\frac{h}{n\theta}\right)^{-n}\longrightarrow e^{-h/\theta}, \qquad \text{balanced error}\longrightarrow\frac12e^{-h/\theta}.

The limit lies strictly between zero and one half. Thus an endpoint difference on the 1/n1/n scale retains nontrivial discrimination in this model.

For an arithmetic illustration, choose θ and h both equal to ten. With one hundred observations, the alternative endpoint is 10.1 and the error is about 0.185. As n grows, the error approaches e⁻¹/2, about 0.184, while the endpoint difference shrinks. These are model calculations, not measurements from an experiment.

At a larger difference h/nh/\sqrt n, the same test's error instead tends to zero. The square-root scale is therefore not the smallest scale that retains discrimination here. That does not disprove square-root conclusions in models whose assumptions justify them. It disproves their unrestricted use across different experiments.

Keep local and fixed alternatives separate

If δ is fixed while n grows, q_n decays exponentially. If δ changes with n, a different limiting problem is being asked. A theorem for fixed alternatives cannot be silently transferred to the second comparison.

Dependence, measurement noise, a different distribution family or a different decision can change the information in each observation. A noisy instrument may erase the sharp boundary that makes this calculation possible.

MONAD's formal testing work includes this moving-support counterexample. Its particular resource consequence comes from the sharp boundary: each sample has an opportunity to enter a region the original hypothesis cannot produce. Changing that opportunity changes what another sample is worth. Sample count becomes informative through the observation model, and the model's support is part of the detection claim rather than a detail to omit from its reported rate.

Testing two uniform endpoints

Let PP be uniform on [0,θ][0,\theta] and QQ uniform on [0,θ+δ][0,\theta+\delta], with θ,δ>0\theta,\delta>0. Observe nn independent samples. On the common region A=[0,θ]nA=[0,\theta]^n, their joint densities are

fP=θ−n,fQ=(θ+δ)−n.f_P=\theta^{-n},\qquad f_Q=(\theta+\delta)^{-n}.

Outside AA, only QQ has positive density. The probability of AA under QQ is

qn=(θθ+δ)n.q_n=\left(\frac{\theta}{\theta+\delta}\right)^n.

With equal priors and unit loss for either mistake, selecting PP on AA and QQ outside it minimises error pointwise. The resulting risk is qn/2q_n/2: the rule never errs under PP, and errs under QQ exactly on AA.

The same overlap calculation gives the normalised total-variation distance

TV⁡(P⊗n,Q⊗n)=1−qn.\operatorname{TV}(P^{\otimes n},Q^{\otimes n})=1-q_n.

Indeed, the overlap integral ∫min⁡(fP,fQ)\int\min(f_P,f_Q) equals qnq_n, since the smaller density on AA is the constant QQ density and there is no overlap outside AA.

Unequal priors change the decision

Let the priors be aa for PP and bb for QQ, with a+b=1a+b=1. On AA, compare afPaf_P with bfQbf_Q; outside it, choose QQ. The optimal risk is

Rn=∫min⁡(afP,bfQ)=min⁡(a,bqn).R_n=\int\min(af_P,bf_Q)=\min(a,bq_n).

If a<bqna<bq_n, even a sample entirely within the smaller interval does not outweigh the prior preference for QQ, and always selecting QQ attains risk aa. Otherwise the support-boundary rule attains risk bqnbq_n.

For a local alternative δ=h/n\delta=h/n with h>0h>0 fixed,

qn=(1+hnθ)−n⟶e−h/θ,Rn⟶min⁡(a,be−h/θ).q_n=\left(1+\frac{h}{n\theta}\right)^{-n}\longrightarrow e^{-h/\theta},\qquad R_n\longrightarrow\min(a,be^{-h/\theta}).

items.title: What can you distinguish with one more move?
items.content_html:
What can you distinguish with one more move?

What does looking again add? An object may reveal nothing new from the same position, but one allowed move can bring another feature into view. Two states indistinguishable at a glance can separate during a short investigation. The observer's resources now belong inside the description of what it can know: the next view costs something, and paying for it changes which views remain possible.

Consider three bits (a,b,c). The observer can read only the first position. It can also rotate the state to (b,c,a), paying one unit per rotation. Reading is free in this toy model, and doing nothing is allowed.

With each affordable rotation, another coordinate becomes observable:

The state space did not grow. The accessible question family grew. At budget one, states 000000 and 001001 remain indistinguishable even though their third bits differ. After one rotation, the third bit sits one more paid move away.

Spending the budget changes what remains possible

Suppose two states agree on every observation reachable with budget two. After one rotation they must still agree on every observation reachable with the remaining budget one. Any such observation can be prefixed with the rotation to form a question already covered by the original budget.

Write x∼Byx\sim_B y when all observations affordable with budget BB agree. If an action uu costs k≤Bk\leq B, then the residual-budget law is

x∼By⟹u(x)∼B−ku(y). x\sim_B y\quad\Longrightarrow\quad u(x)\sim_{B-k}u(y).

A separating continuation of cost at most B−kB-k would, when prefixed by uu, separate the original states within budget BB. That contradicts the premise. Reusing the full original budget after the move would smuggle in an extra resource allocation.

The example assumes deterministic total actions, state-independent non-negative costs and a declared set of observations. If an action sometimes fails, costs depend on the state or measurements disturb it, those features have to enter the model.

Accessibility is different from retention

The observer might have access to the full three-bit state but currently lack the budget to inspect it. The bits are hidden from that observer's present protocol, not erased. Alternatively, a store might have retained only a and discarded b and c. Rotating that one-bit summary does not recreate the original state.

An archive or a fresh measurement could make the missing bits available. Its storage, access permission, transfer and latency are part of the repair. The distinction between “I have not looked” and “I no longer have it” is as important for a retrieval system as it is for this finite model.

More resources do not necessarily mean one scalar

Three-bit rotation uses one simple cost. Real investigations may be limited by memory, compute, bandwidth, trials and elapsed time. A procedure using less memory but more communication is not automatically cheaper. A larger allowance can bring another query within reach, but only if its source remains accessible.

A useful comparison first names which resources can substitute for one another, which are hard ceilings and which measurements actually require them. Otherwise a claim of greater distinguishability may merely have changed the accounting unit.

The broader MONAD question asks how descriptions remain adequate as their admissible questions change. This example makes one part tractable: future questions can be indexed by a finite cost, and spending that cost changes the remaining comparison. The observer's representation is now tied to a protocol with an allowance, rather than to a glance treated as the whole investigation. Choosing among those reads introduces repair cost: an affordable first question may leave an expensive distinction unresolved.

The residual-budget argument

Let XX be a finite state space. Each admitted action aa is a total deterministic map Ta:X→XT_a:X\to X with a state-independent cost c(a)≥0c(a)\geq0. A word ww is a finite sequence of actions, TwT_w applies them in sequence, and c(w)c(w) is the sum of their costs. Include the empty word, with identity action and zero cost. Let PP be the set of observations the observer may make, its probes.

For a budget b≥0b\geq0, define

x∼by⟺p(Twx)=p(Twy) for every p∈P and w with c(w)≤b.x\sim_b y\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p(T_wx)=p(T_wy)\text{ for every }p\in P\text{ and }w\text{ with }c(w)\leq b.

This is an equivalence relation: it is agreement on a family of functions. If b′≤bb'\leq b, then x∼byx\sim_b y implies x∼b′yx\sim_{b'}y, because every word admitted by the smaller budget is also admitted by the larger one.

Now apply an action aa with c(a)≤bc(a)\leq b. Any word ww affordable afterwards has c(w)≤b−c(a)c(w)\leq b-c(a). Applying aa first and then ww costs at most bb, so the original equivalence gives

p(Tw(Tax))=p(Tw(Tay)).p(T_w(T_ax))=p(T_w(T_ay)).

Thus Tax∼b−c(a)TayT_ax\sim_{b-c(a)}T_ay. If qbq_b maps a state to its equivalence class, this defines a well-defined map between two different quotients:

The change of quotient is essential. In the rotation example, 000 and 001 agree at budget one: both expose a=0 and b=0. Rotate them to 000 and 010. At a fresh budget one, the states differ because the next rotation exposes the original third bit. At the correct remaining budget zero, both still expose zero. Keeping budget one on the right side would grant a second paid rotation.

State-dependent costs require a model that carries the remaining resource state. Partial actions also require an explicit account of admission and failure. The proof above uses totality and a common cost bound to ensure that the same prefixed word is available in both states; it cannot simply discard those hypotheses.

items.title: Compression is a promise about questions
items.content_html:
Compression is a promise about questions

Yesterday's summary answered every question we asked of it. Today we need one more answer, and the summary gives two different situations the same name. It has not necessarily become inaccurate. Its earlier success concealed a choice about which differences were worth keeping. Can we locate that choice precisely enough to know what the new question needs?

Take four states, represented by two bits. Suppose the only question is whether the first bit is one. The summary q(a,b)=aq(a,b)=a answers it perfectly:

Original state Summary qq First-bit answer Second-bit answer
0000 00 00 00
0101 00 00 11
1010 11 11 00
1111 11 11 11

It keeps two classes, {00,01}\{00,01\} and {10,11}\{10,11\}, instead of four states. Nothing relevant to the first question has been lost. The final column shows exactly what the summary cannot recover.

Now ask whether the second bit is one. The old summary cannot answer. Both 00 and 01 became 0, but their answers differ. There is no function of that single retained bit which returns both answers correctly. More computation, a more persuasive explanation and a larger language model cannot repair this exact ambiguity from the same input alone.

The question family defines the summary

Write a question as a function ff on the original states. It can be answered from a summary qq when some function gg satisfies

f=g∘q. f=g\circ q.

For a surjective summary, this is equivalent to ff being constant on every group of states that qq merged. Necessity follows because equal summaries give gg the same input. For sufficiency, choose any representative of a summary class and return its answer; constancy makes the choice irrelevant. This is the small proof behind the promise.

The second bit existed before anybody asked about it. Making it relevant changed the question family, not the state space. A richer language capable of representing previously unavailable objects would pose a further problem; the two-bit example isolates the simpler change so that its consequence can be calculated exactly.

An agent's notes have the same vulnerability. They can be excellent for the task that produced them and inadequate for a new task. Understanding which answers they preserve lets the agent recognise that inadequacy before it turns an ambiguous record into a confident response. The missing distinction points towards what another read or measurement would need to supply.

A publication gives this a practical form. A listing can keep an article's title, description and address while leaving out its argument. That is enough to choose something to read. It is not enough to check a proof: two revisions can keep the same listing while one changes the crucial step. Gazette keeps the authored article as the source and derives the listing from it, so the reader can follow the address to the reasoning. The short description serves discovery; the retained article makes a deeper question answerable. If only the listing survived, no amount of searching those three fields would recover the missing step.

Repair needs an information source

Several repairs are possible, and they have different costs. Retaining the original two bits preserves both answers directly; a supplement containing the second bit restores just the missing distinction. Measuring the original object again can supply that bit if the object still exists and the measurement is permitted. Without one of these sources, declining to answer preserves the boundary between an unresolved question and a guess presented as reconstruction.

In this example, preserving the ability to answer both coordinate questions requires distinguishing all four states. A binary supplement with two values suffices because each old summary class contains two states. This is finite alphabet accounting, not a coding theorem about an arbitrary stream, and it assumes the supplement's encoder had access to the original state.

The question sits near established mathematics of abstraction. Cousot and Cousot's abstract interpretation studies computation through abstractions; an exact correspondence would locate which existing constructions a changing-question account can reuse and where its additional obligations begin.

An exact supplement and a noisy observation make different promises. A report can be informative while leaving both original states possible. Repeated measurements may reduce a decision's error, but improving the chance of being right is not the same as restoring the answer in every state.

The future cannot be unrestricted for free

If every possible question separating every pair of states must remain answerable, a sufficient summary cannot merge any two states. Perfect future safety then removes nontrivial compression. A useful system must choose a restricted family, tolerate an explicit approximation, retain a repair source or accept that some later questions will remain unanswered.

The two-bit construction gives the changing-description problem a small but useful starting point: a summary's failure can be identified as a particular unanswered question, and a repair can be specified by the distinction it must restore. With budgeted continuations, the future family also depends on what the observer can afford to do next. The summary and the remaining access together determine which promise can still be kept.

01	0	0	1	
10	1	1	0	
11	1	1	1
